summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free web app that shows, for any lunar south pole landing site and date, whether a lander will have sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for communication. It combines Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons with terrain horizons we computed from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data, so the Sun and Earth are judged against the real crater walls and ridges, not a flat horizon. Mission planners, educators and the public can compare sites side by side, compare landing dates at one site, see countdowns to sunset and Earthset, and analyse their own coordinates.
Near the pole the Sun stays only a few degrees above the horizon, so terrain decides everything. Over two years, Shackleton's rim is sunlit about 91% of the time, while Haworth's rim sees Earth only about 2% of the time, because the Malapert massif 16.6 km away blocks it. When a launch slips, a team can re-check sites and dates in seconds instead of navigating several specialist tools.
details:
What it does. For four south pole sites (Shackleton rim, de Gerlache rim, Malapert massif, Haworth rim) and any custom coordinates, the app shows:

  • a 360° horizon view with the Sun and Earth moving against the real skyline
  • the solar elevation angle and the share of the Sun's disk above the terrain
  • GO / NO-GO status for power and direct-to-Earth communication
  • countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset
  • a timeline of power and communication windows from December 2026 to December 2028
  • comparison cards for several sites, or for one site on different landing dates, plus "Suggest best dates"
  • a south polar map with LOLA shaded relief and permanently shadowed regions
  • adjustable planning margins, shareable links, image and CSV export, and a guided tour for newcomers

How it works.

  1. Sun and Earth positions: one JPL Horizons query gives the sub-solar point, the sub-Earth point (libration included) and the Earth–Moon distance every hour. From these, the app computes Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation for any site in the browser, including a parallax correction for Earth.
  2. Terrain horizons: from the 80 m/px LOLA south polar elevation model, we trace 360 directions from each site out to the edge of the model, 2 m above the ground, correct for the Moon's curvature, and keep the highest terrain angle in each direction. Custom locations use a 10 km grid of precomputed horizons.
  3. Site positions: each site is a flat spot (slope under 5° at 80 m resolution) checked against the elevation model to sit on its crater rim or massif top.
  4. The app: a static web page (no server) on GitHub Pages compares the Sun and Earth with the horizon at every time step.

Validation. Our ephemeris matches Horizons' own surface-observer azimuth and elevation to within 0.0004° in elevation and 0.0055° in azimuth. The app's math matches an independent 3-D vector calculation to within 0.005°. Maximum Sun elevations match the theoretical limit for each latitude. An automated validator checks every data file on every change.

Benefits. Rapid, visual trade-offs between sites and dates for planners, without specialist software. An honest picture of uncertainty: the app labels coarse terrain and states its limits. For educators and the public, it makes clear why the lunar south pole is so hard: a 5 km move from Shackleton's rim changes the horizon by up to 32°.

What we hope to achieve. A tool that helps teams respond quickly when schedules or hardware force a change of landing date or site, and helps students understand why lunar mission planning is so complex.

Limits. This is a screening aid, not a mission-grade model. "Earth visible" means Earth's centre is above the skyline (geometry, not a link budget). Times are hourly. Slopes are measured at 80 m resolution and don't guarantee a safe landing spot. Custom locations near crater rims are rough.
Creativity. Most tools judge sunlight against a flat horizon or need specialist software. We put Sun, Earth and real terrain in one interactive horizon view that anyone can open in a browser, and we turned two years of hourly geometry into simple GO / NO-GO signals and countdowns.
Factors we considered. Accuracy versus speed (precomputing horizons so the app runs with no server), honest limits instead of false precision, the observer height above the ground, the Moon’s curvature, the edge of the elevation model, and making the tool usable for planners and newcomers alike.

Tools and languages. Python (numpy, scipy, matplotlib, rasterio, pyproj, requests, Pillow) for the data pipeline; HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework for the app; GitHub, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages; Google Fonts (Barlow, Barlow Condensed).
